title: Part 1
text: Chapter One – Drip Feed Trials always seemed to start the same: sharp inhale, tug behind the ribs, then boots on asphalt and the hum of the Fog fading off. Dwight blinked against the gray light of the Bedham Preschool domain. The air already felt heavier here, like the whole world had exhaled but never breathed back in. The Fog deposited them separately, the way it sometimes did — Dwight materializing at the far end of the street, David a half-block down and already scanning the sightlines before he'd fully arrived. They found each other without incident. A quick glance around told them they were alone at the moment; the others having been dropped in somewhere else. That was fine. Normal. Survivors rarely arrived as a full set, and Badham's twisted little playground was familiar enough not to panic about. The preschool sat low against the grey sky, its painted murals faded to suggestions of color, the chain-link fence around the yard sagging in places where rust had won the argument with the metal. Neither of them had pulled Bedham in a while, the Entity seeming to favor the woodsier domains as of late for some reason. Dwight tried to remember if there was anything particular about the layout worth flagging and came up mostly empty. Standard build. Tight interior. The basement generator was the move — killers avoided it because the pipe hallway that divided the lower level into two rooms was a nightmare to navigate, all jutting valves and blind corners, and there were two ways up instead of one. It was the kind of start that let you bank some early progress before things went sideways, turning chases into slow collisions and smug laughter. You could get a gen nearly done before they even thought about trying. It was the easiest way to relax before the real chases started. Get your bearings, work out the rust from joints. So long as the killer wasn’t one of the teleporting ones, it should be easy enough. David seemed to be running the same thought, as he sized up the immediate area, took one look at the weathered shell of the preschool and sighed, squaring his shoulders. “Boiler room?” “Boiler room,” Dwight echoed. They crossed the threshold into the school, ducking under a rusted EXIT sign that had long since given up. Bedham never had doors — none of the buildings seemed to — just openings where the idea of a door had been removed, neat rectangles cut through plaster and expectation. Dwight had stopped finding it strange years ago — the absence of doors was just part of the grammar of this place, the particular way the Entity assembled things from memory and suggestion rather than reality. The hall beyond breathed dust. Paper curls clung to a corkboard with sun-bleached pushpins. A child’s drawing of a house had flaked down to a white outline of someplace else. Light pooled in thin yellow lines through warped blinds, and dust swirled lazily in the shafts like it was still caught mid-class. A noise from deeper in — something heavy scraping tile; a crash of furniture meeting wall — made both of them drop without thinking, pressing back against the hallway lockers. A second sound followed, wood on metal, unnecessary and dramatic. David angled Dwight behind him on reflex, only to freeze when the source revealed itself down the far corridor: Ghostface, draped in black and carelessly visible, filming his own vandalism as if bored by the lack of applause. He shoved a locker door until it bounced back, then flicked his phone toward it like he was rating the performance. He wasn't stalking. He wasn't even paying attention to the building around him, which was the only reason he hadn't already seen them. He was filming himself on his phone with one hand and picking up a small plastic chair with the other, examining it with the critical eye of someone who had found something deeply disappointing. He turned it over once, seemed to find it lacking, and hurled it sideways into the wall with a hollow clatter that echoed the length of the building. “Just Ghostface,” he muttered with a small eyeroll, shaking his head lightly as the tension left his shoulders. “Looks like he’s in one of his moods.” Dwight nodded. The relief came with a small, wry exhale. A visible killer was a polite killer. Danny’s menace lived in the corners — no point wasting fear when he was being obvious. As long as he wasn’t looking their way, who cared? If the killer was already goofing around like this, he was clearly not in the mood to do a proper hunt. So long as everyone stayed out of his line of sight, they should be fine. Had he actually cared today, he would have been stealthed, and they might have missed him entirely. Danny moved on down the far corridor without once looking their way, already pointing his phone at something else. The faint sound of his own commentary floated back to them, too distant to make out. They gave it a moment before moving again. They took the opposite stairwell, easing down into the basement beneath flickering bulbs and rust-streaked walls. Dwight tried not to notice the way his shoulder brushed the wall with every step. It felt narrower than it should’ve, but that was just adrenaline. It had to be. It was a preschool, after all. Made for small bodies. It didn’t help that Danny's terror radius had a particular weight to it, a low crawling pressure that played tricks if you let it. Even on the other side of the building, it thrummed uncomfortably against his chest. That’s all this was, most likely. Just nerves. The generator waited at the far wall—half-skinned, half-sunk in a trap of its own piping. Dwight’s hands found the familiar metal and the familiar thrill of making something uncooperative do what it was told. It caught on the third try, settled into its familiar grind, and they fell into the rhythm of it without needing to discuss it. Sparks jumped and died. The hum of effort thrummed through the casing into his palms. David set opposite him, matching rhythm without comment. The work made sense. It borrowed your brain and filled it with timing. It felt good to be able to ignore the usual tension of a trial for a bit and just do something repetitive. For a while, that was enough. Snap. Click. Turn. Hold. Routine. And yet... something itched under Dwight’s skin almost immediately. Dwight frowned against the odd ambience. A strange noise, he could understand. That kind of thing was common, if concerning in of itself. This though? This felt...weird. The basement had a quality to its silence that didn't sit right — not the comfortable quiet of a space with nobody in it, but something closer to held breath. Could always be just the generator dampening other sounds, he mused. Normally he didn’t notice that effect, but he also didn’t usually have the time to stop and listen to the area around him for long before needing to run or hide. Shaking off the eeriness, Dwight shifted his position slightly and tried to focus back on what he was doing. If he let his mind wander too much, he could miss a spark, and the killer would DEFINITELY hear a generator misfire. Even Danny couldn’t ignore that kind of a blast. The ground made an odd sound as his shoe slid across it, drawing his eye back away from the wires again. The floor felt damp beneath his shoes. Not unusual, not really, but... more than usual. Glancing down, his foot gently rippled an inch, maybe two, of stagnant water; glossy and brown-green in the anemic light. It lay so still it had filmed over, surface tension tempering it into glass. His shoes had been sitting in it long enough that his socks were already damp at the heel. He somehow hadn't noticed. The walls seemed just as saturated, a faint sheen of moisture on the concrete like the whole room was slowly exhaling — and the scent that hung on everything was low and wet and old, mold and rust and something underneath both that he didn't have a name for. The air pressed in humid and hot, and one of the nearby pipes hissed like a living thing, sending steam drifting lazily through the room. Was it always this...wet? His breath went shallow for one beat, and then he smoothed it with reason. Basements flooded. Old buildings leaked. Pressure lines failed. The Entity was many things, but OSHA- compliant was not one of them. Though there had never been a leak like this before, he was sure of that. Even at it’s worst, the preschool was run down and broken. Never... moist. The overhead light buzzed, as if agreeing with his discomfort. It didn't flicker the way the lights usually did when a generator was running — that particular feedback was almost soothing by now, a sign that the work was registering. This was a flat, lazy drone, the light steady and somehow worse for it. The sickly light somehow managed to make everything look just a little bit off. Even the opening to the pipe hallway seemed to sit at the wrong angle. Dwight glared at the hallway, generator forgotten as the wrongness seeped into his bones, his eyes snagging on a proportion that didn't resolve correctly no matter how long he looked at it. The doorframe was fine. The hallway beyond it was fine. But the relationship between them was off somehow, stretched or rotated by a degree or two in a direction that geometry didn't technically have a name for. David didn’t seem to notice. Or maybe he just didn’t care. His entire frame was steady, eyes glued on his work, hands moving with the practiced ease of someone who had done this entirely too many times. Dwight flexed his fingers and tried to keep working, but his eyes kept tracking the edges of the room. There were flickers in the lights of most trials, sure. Ambient smells and noises that were meant to set off nerves, naturally. Still... There shouldn’t be standing water. That part he was sure of. But when he squinted down, there it was: ripples, shallow and lazy. Maybe an inch, maybe more. He was still trying to find the words for it, contemplating asking if David was noticing it too, when the pipe went. The sound cracked through the basement like a gunshot — something rupturing deep in the hallway, a violent hiss of pressure releasing all at once — and David was on his feet before the echo died. A sharp inhale punched through his teeth as he spun, one hand shooting back as if to block Dwight, ready to fend off whatever was attacking. The pipe at the far end of the hallway was weeping a dark stain down the wall, and that was all. No attacker, no disaster. Just a blown pipe. He stood there for a beat, chest rising fast, then turned, half embarrassed, half bewildered, already opening his mouth to get Dwight back on task and hopefully not harassing him for being jumpy. He froze mid syllable at his teammate’s expression. Dwight wasn't looking at him. He was still staring at the pipe hallway opening, the generator humming under his idle hands, with a stillness that made David’s hair stand on end. Clearly the man had spotted something he had missed while trying to fight absolutely nothing? David followed his gaze, not seeing anything new, and turned back to the generator with an annoyed huff. This place was clearly getting to them both. Best to get the generator done and get back upstairs before their nerves went off even worse than they already are. Dwight was anxious to start with, and David was really not interested in that anxiety rubbing off on him right now. “Hey. Earth to Dwight?” Dwight blinked and looked away. “Sorry. Just... weird feeling.” He shifted his stance. Slosh. He looked down. “...When the fuck did this place have a wading pool?” The water lapped above the arch of his foot. It had soaked through his socks. Not just wet...murky. Almost oily. It caught what little light the buzzing overhead fixture offered, dark and absolutely still. How had he not noticed that? It wasn’t very deep, but it was more than enough that he should have noticed while he was elbow deep in generator grease. So how the fuck did he MISS that? He took another look around the room, lightly clenching one fist in idle twitchiness from the mix of mold smell and the persistent heavy heartbeat thrum from the killer upstairs. That was enough. There were other generators in other buildings and none of them were currently trying to give him a feeling he couldn't shake. They could leave this one to whoever else had pulled Bedham tonight and go find something less — whatever this was. “Right. Nope. I’m out.” He backed away from the generator with abrupt finality. “Too wet. Too quiet. Too weird. I’m not getting trench foot for a basement gen. Back upstairs. We can go do one of the 2nd story house gens. You with me?” Dwight blinked, pulled his attention back. “Yeah. Sorry.” He shook out his hands as if they’d gone numb. “We can do a different house. It’s—” He made a face. “—gross down here.” “Gross I can do,” David said. “This is... extra.” He flicked a glance toward the stairs they’d come down. “Let’s try upstairs before it turns into any more of a sauna.” He took a breath to ask if David felt it too, if the room was wrong, if he’d imagined the hallway getting longer; but David was already headed for the stairs. Dwight put a palm on the wall as he reached the bottom step, and the concrete felt warmer than it should have. Body-warm. He wiped his hand on his jeans and pretended the fabric hadn’t already stuck to his knee. David made it partway up before slipping back into a crouch and pressing against the wall before the stairs bent to go up. Danny was sitting at the top, just above the landing. Phone in hand. Legs swinging lazily. Silently thumbing through an app like he was waiting for a bus. Not stealthed, not hunting — just there, in the worst possible place, with all the awareness of someone who had never seriously considered that anything might be coming up those stairs toward him. David waved Dwight back, patting his chest quick and pointing up. Terror heartbeat straight ahead. Of course, the killer would be right there. It would be their luck that Danny had gotten bored with trashing the place and had settled in to play games on his phone for half a trial. The boys shared a look, weighing options. The basement, with its wrong angles and weird light and inch of standing water, waited behind them. These stairs were clearly a no-go. That left the pipe hallway hole and the far back steps. The hole in the hallway ceiling wasn’t reachable from the ground, and even if they could scramble up to it, the hall it was in was directly down from the stairs. Trying to pass by Ghostface with a clear line of sight was a gamble at the best of times. Dude was entirely too quick and wily. “Other stairs,” David mouthed silently, jerking his chin towards the pipe hallway. Dwight nodded briskly and followed David into the mini-maze, only relaxing slightly when the terror radius calmed from a panicked hammering into a background thump, before fading away entirely. The air in the hallway was worse; stale and wet and sharp, the kind of smell that curled behind your eyes. Pipes creaked above them, old and half-rotted. Twice, they had to duck surprise sprays of water as valves burst open in sharp, echoing snaps. The steam made the walls sweat. Dwight had almost immediately lost all sense of the room's geometry. The hallway had always been easy to get turned around in — he knew that, had been in it before — but something about the proportions felt wrong in a way that went beyond the usual tangle of valves and junctions. The walls were the right color, the pipes were the right rust, and somehow none of it added up to a space that felt like it should exist. Valves hissed as they passed. One of them let out a sudden spray that soaked David’s shoulder, making him flinch and swear again. “Didn’t this used to be a lot shorter?” “Layout changes,” Dwight murmured, slightly relieved that it wasn’t just him that had noticed. “It happens. The domains shift sometimes. Usually between trials, but..." He trailed off, looking at the way the hallway kept going into the dark past the edge of what the light could reach. "Usually between trials." “Yeah, well, I don’t like this version.” There was no echo to their footfalls anymore. Just wet slaps swallowed by the space. David kept glancing at the pipes, brow furrowed in clear distrust, murmuring half to himself. The second room was somehow worse than the first. The water had found their ankles somewhere in the pipe hallway and followed them through, and by the time they cleared the last junction it was sitting just above — cool against the humid press of the air, which was somehow both damp and warm in a way that made no sense for a basement. The overhead light buzzed its flat, dying note. Dwight looked up, but the bulb wasn’t flickering. It was just making that sound anyway, as it cast oddly angled shadows over the lockers that lined the wall. The stairs were gone. Not literally, but effectively. A wall of furniture had been shoved into the stairwell. Desks stacked against shelving units stacked against lockers, the whole mass of stuff settling into the stairwell opening like it had grown there. Some pieces looked warped. Wet. Some wedged. Some clearly just tossed. All crammed into the stairwell as if the building had tried to eat itself. The furniture was preschool sized mostly, but there was enough of it packed in that the combined weight was something else entirely. There was no space to squeeze through. No handholds. Overhead, the lone light in the ceiling dimmed with a jittery flicker before settling into its usual brightness. "That's what he was doing," Dwight murmured, mostly to himself. The scraping sounds from upstairs when they first came in. Danny throwing things around. They'd assumed boredom. They hadn't been wrong, exactly. David was already at the stack, shoulder against the nearest locker, pushing. The locker didn't move. He reset his footing and pushed harder. The furniture shifted — just slightly, a quarter inch of give — and then settled back exactly as it had been, as if the gap had never existed. David stared at it, dumfounded. Pushed again. Same result. He tried a desk next, getting his fingers under the edge and hauling upward. The desk rocked once and came back down with a muffled sound that the air swallowed before it could properly echo, and David pulled his shoulder back with a sharp exhale, rolling it once. "Brilliant. Just... great. The hell even IS this?” “More importantly, how’d we not hear it? This should have made a ton of noise. We couldn’t have been more than 50 feet away. Tops. I know the hallway eats sound in the corners, but there should have been something.” They tried to clear the stairs, pulling one chair, then another, but everything they dislodged seemed to drag more with it. Like the pile was settling, not shrinking. Several of the heavier pieces wouldn’t budge at all. He took a breath and shoved again. The metal scraped, and the sound came out small, politely swallowed by the air. He stepped back with a scowl and flexed his fingers. Dwight tried a chair leg, then another, testing angles for leverage. The sounds were wrong. That was the thing that kept nagging at Dwight as the two worked methodically through their options — wrong in a specific, deliberate way. When David's shoulder connected with the locker, the impact made a sound that didn't carry. When the furniture shifted and settled back, the scrape of it was swallowed before it could reach the walls. The basement should have been bouncing noise around, hard floors and concrete and all that pipe — instead everything just landed flat, absorbed, like the air itself had decided sound wasn't worth keeping. Dwight stood in the water and listened to the silence eating itself for a moment longer. He almost mentioned it, then thought better of it. David already looked like he was getting annoyed with the stairway plug. Bringing up one more bit of weirdness in all this was not likely to land in his favor. Dwight glanced back the way they came. “Should we go back? Danny gets bored easily; maybe he moved?” David looked back at him over his shoulder, expression unreadable. "Worth checking," Dwight murmured lightly, with slightly less conviction. David nudged a shelf with his boot, barely listening, then hissed a breath through his teeth and shook his foot as if something in the water had touched him. “Nope. Don’t like that.” Dwight looked through the mouth of the pipe hall again. The corridor lurched longer while he watched it — only a fraction, only the kind of shift you can blame on a blink. Looking back to try and get David’s attention again, he noticed the stiffness in his shoulders and realized he had seen it too. The decision settled around them both. It was time to go. Now. That was when the pipes screamed. Somewhere deeper down the pipe hall, something ruptured — a sharp concussive crack followed immediately by a sustained shriek of pressure, the sound of it tearing through the basement — and both of them ducked on instinct, water soaking into clothing and rippling against random debris around them, Dwight's hands finding the nearest pipe junction, David crouched low with his arms thrown over his head, both of them braced for something that didn't come. Steam burst out from a seam to their left and hit the ceiling in a white bloom that didn’t disperse correctly. The bulb above them stuttered as if it had hiccupped on its own heat. Once. Twice. The third time, it simply failed, plunging the entire basement into an oppressive darkness. The building held its breath. Chapter Two – Floodline Darkness fell and did not lift. There was no flicker. No emergency backup. No lingering hum of standby power. One moment, the overhead light buzzed, warped and sickly, and the next, it was gone. The darkness just was — thick and absolute, a total absence that clung to their skin like wet cloth, pressing in from all sides until the two of them were just breathing in it and trying to remember where the walls were. Dwight couldn’t tell where his skin stopped and the world began. The water had reached his shins, warm in a way that felt wrong — closer to body temperature than anything a basement had a right to be. A splash to his right; David swore under his breath, reaching out for something solid to orient himself, and caught his shoulder hard on a locker. The sound it made was flat and brief and immediately gone. The water sloshed violently at the impact, licking up Dwight’s calves and soaking the fabric that hadn’t already glued to him. “You good?” Dwight called into the void. “Peachy,” David grunted. “Don’t suppose you’ve got a light?” Dwight patted his jacket, and his fingers bumped the slim cylinder tucked in the inside pocket. Relief buzzed through him. “Yeah — hang on—” The flashlight slipped as he tried to pull it free, fingers fumbling, nerves not quite obeying. He caught it on the second grab and thumbed it on. The beam sputtered. Then held. Barely. It cast a cone of weak yellow light maybe a foot and a half ahead — just enough to see David’s outline, slick with water and tension. The shadows pressed in thick around the edges, greedy and reluctant to let anything through. “Better than nothing,” he rubbed at his shoulder where he had caught it in the dark. “Goddamn lockers.” David turned toward the barricade, the light barely outlining the mess of desks and shelves still wedged into the stairwell. “I’m not wandering blind,” he said. “I’m gonna try moving this crap again. Just one desk. Just one fucking desk and I can climb over the rest.” He planted his feet in the water and shoved. The stack shifted and resettled. He shoved again. Same result. He worked his way along the pile, trying different points of leverage, each impact swallowed before it could properly echo, the sounds dying the moment they left his hands like they were ashamed of themselves. He very pointedly did not say anything about that. “Fuck’s sake.” He stepped back, kicked a locker. The metal thunk was dull. Muffled. Like it had been swallowed by insulation. Dwight barely heard it. He was inching along the wall again, one hand trailing rust-damp metal as he backtracked toward the pipe hallway. The flashlight shivered in his grip as he swept it across the darkness. He turned, slipping slightly as the water surged with his motion. He nearly dropped the flashlight. Caught it with both hands and steadied his breath. David had both hands locked on a locker handle now, wrenching hard. Something groaned behind it but didn’t give. “Why can’t I hear anything?” David muttered. “I’m making noise, I know I am.” Dwight didn’t answer. He was still staring at the water. The whole basement was dark, sure — but the water was darker, somehow. Not just murky. The light caught the surface and went nowhere, reflected back like the water had decided it wasn't interested in being seen through. Something grazed his shin. He flinched hard, flashlight jerking up and sending spastic light darts along the ceiling. He spun in place slowly, sweeping the beam down again. It barely cut the surface, but it was darker than it should have been. Murkier. It wasn’t just dirty — it was opaque, metallic, like it had decided reflection was another way out and sealed it. Like more than just rust was bleeding through the pipes. Nothing there. Obviously, nothing there. The water found his calves while he was still trying to convince himself of that. The beam barely penetrated an inch before giving up entirely, which was either a property of the water or a property of the flashlight, and he wasn't sure which option was worse. The Nothing bumped his calf. Gentle. Almost curious. His breath hitched. “David?” David didn’t look up. He had both hands on a large desk, hauling upward with everything he had. The desk rocked — genuinely rocked this time, a real shift, the stack above it grinding with what sounded almost like progress — and then slid smoothly back into place as if he'd never touched it. “David, I think there’s something in the water,” Dwight whispered. David glanced back, shadowed eyes narrow. “Debris. Keep your head.” David gave the desk another shove. It rocked, then slid back into place as if correcting itself. “Debris doesn’t do that.” "I've nearly got it." He didn't have it. Dwight could see that plainly. But David's jaw was set in the particular way it got when he'd decided something was happening through sheer force of will, and interrupting that with there might be something in the water with us was not a conversation Dwight felt equipped to have right now. David simply shoved the barricade again, muscles bunching under soaked cloth. Another scrape, another futile give. The water rippled outward and came back against them both. The water had reached his knees at some point without Dwight noticing, the warmth of it creeping upward so gradually that his body had simply accepted it. Something grazed the inside of his knee — higher than before — and he locked every muscle in his body simultaneously, the flashlight beam skittering sideways as his hand jerked. Nothing. Dark water. Pipes. His own heartbeat loud enough to hear. Minutes — maybe longer — passed in the churn of their own breathing. The beam quivered between them like a nervous heartbeat. Then the furniture groaned. A shelf slid down from the top of the pile and hit the water without a splash. The air absorbed the sound. — The water was up to their waists when David finally gave up on the stairwell. The stack above David shifted, and a cascade of debris came down to fill the gap he'd made. He stepped back, breathing hard, and looked at his hands. Knuckles scraped raw. His shoulder had graduated from bruised to something more insistent. The stairwell stared back at him, unchanged and utterly indifferent to everything he'd put into it. A shelf tumbled down from the plug and landed with a wet thud, nearly hitting him. "It’s not giving," he spat, kicking one of the desks hard enough to jar his shin. Dwight’s light jittered across the walls. He tried not to look at the water anymore. He didn’t want to see it. “We should go back. Try the first stairs. At least those were open.” “Are you sure he’s moved on?” “No...” Dwight cast the beam into the pipe hall for a moment, shuddering lightly at the way the light seemed to be eaten in the distance. “But it’s not like we can just stay here.” David gave a long, ragged sigh, finally stepping back from the mass of furniture
